criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household and community clean/piped water service access in Jakarta, including city-wide piped water coverage, unmet connection targets for low-income communities, and informal water vendor or groundwater reliance among the urban poor in informal settlements.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Plain reading: yes, examines water governance, PPP contracting, regulatory oversight, and remunicipalization. Narrow 2026-10-13 reading: yes, directly examines utility ownership and contractual/regulatory structure governing service access (specifically Jakarta's 1998-2023 25-year PPP Build-Operate-Transfer concession contracts, unfavorable contractual clauses, 2023 remunicipalization under public utility PAM JAYA, regulatory bodies' inability to enforce service/connection targets and groundwater extraction bans, and tariff/cost-recovery governance), which fall squarely within 'utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access', 'enforcement', and 'tariff or cost-recovery rules' rather than unanalysed macro-governance background.
criterion_notes.c3: Conducts a systematic literature review (systematic empirical synthesis) with an explicit Google Scholar search string (2010-2024 in English and Indonesian), backward snowballing, explicit inclusion/exclusion table (Table 2), PRISMA study selection (n=31 included studies: 27 contemporary and 4 foundational), descriptive study-characteristics breakdown (Table 3), and Braun & Clarke qualitative thematic coding triangulated with government/utility plans. Criterion 3 explicitly includes systematic empirical syntheses; reporting limitations (single search engine, illustrative citations rather than a full 31-study bibliography, and placeholder text in Figure 1) affect methodological quality rather than eligibility.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to water access, connection, exclusion, and affordability/availability: piped water coverage stagnant at approximately 65% of Jakarta's population (leaving a third unserved), failure to meet contractual connection targets for low-income communities, reliance of the urban poor in informal settlements on expensive and unsafe water from informal vendors, ~40% of total water demand met by groundwater extraction, and 40-50% non-revenue water.
criterion_notes.c5: Provides sufficient information to identify the population and units of analysis (Jakarta urban population and low-income/informal-settlement households at the city/utility level; synthesis unit n=31 studies), the institutional/regulatory exposure (PPP concession contracts, regulatory enforcement failures, and 2023 remunicipalization to PAM JAYA), the service-access outcomes, and the study design (systematic literature review with qualitative thematic synthesis). No quantitative effect size is required for review inclusion per Criterion 6.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English (primary literature search covered English and Indonesian studies).

evidence_quotes.quote: With piped water failing to reach a third of the population, a significant portion of residents and industries have resorted to rampant groundwater extraction.

Rather, it was structured as a 25-year Public-Private Partnership (PPP) concession—a form of Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model. This was positioned as a business model innovation aimed at injecting private capital and operational efficiency to expand service coverage in ways the public utility had failed to do [5].

Foundational literature from the 2000s critically identified flaws in the initial design: a lack of transparency, weak regulatory oversight, and unfavorable contractual clauses that limited the government's control [4].
As contemporary studies consistently show [6], [13], regulatory bodies were unable to enforce service targets or groundwater regulations.

The selection process for the primary search is documented in the PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 2). This process yielded 27 contemporary studies. The backward search identified an additional 4 foundational studies from the pre-2010 period, which were integrated directly into the analysis. In total, 31 studies form the evidence base for this review.
Foundational studies highlighted the model's failure to meet connection targets for low-income communities.

Studies like [14] move beyond policy analysis to document the daily reality for the urban poor: dependence on expensive and unsafe water from informal vendors, direct health impacts, and a deepening of the poverty cycle.

raw_response.exposure: 25-year water utility Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Build-Operate-Transfer concession contracts (1998-2023), flawed contractual clauses, weak regulatory oversight and non-enforcement of service connection targets and groundwater extraction bans, and 2023 remunicipalization under public utility PAM JAYA
raw_response.outcome: Piped drinking-water service coverage (stagnant at ~65% of Jakarta's population), unmet universal coverage KPIs and connection targets for low-income communities, socio-economic exclusion of the urban poor resulting in reliance on expensive informal water vendors, groundwater reliance (~40% of city water demand), and non-revenue water (40-50%)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban population and low-income/informal-settlement residents in Jakarta, Indonesia (municipal/utility service system under PAM JAYA and former PPP concessionaires); synthesis sample of n=31 peer-reviewed and foundational studies (4 from 2000-2009; 27 from 2010-2024)
raw_response.rationale: Full-text English systematic literature review (n=31 included studies selected via an explicit search string, eligibility table, and PRISMA workflow, synthesized via thematic coding) examining piped water service access in Jakarta, Indonesia. It satisfies Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 by reporting piped water coverage (~65%), unmet connection targets for low-income communities, and informal-vendor/groundwater reliance among unserved residents. It satisfies Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because it directly examines utility ownership/concession contracting (the 1998-2023 PPP BOT contracts vs. 2023 remunicipalization under PAM JAYA), contractual design flaws, regulatory enforcement of connection targets and groundwater bans, and tariff governance. Criterion 3 explicitly permits systematic empirical syntheses; reporting limitations in this conference paper (single database search, illustrative citations rather than a complete 31-study reference list, and unrendered Figure 1 text) lower confidence to medium rather than warranting exclusion.
raw_response.study_design: Systematic literature review (qualitative thematic synthesis of n=31 studies using PRISMA selection and Braun & Clarke thematic coding, triangulated with national, provincial, and utility strategic documents)
